description: AI Village talks from DEF CON 34.

talks.title: Leveraging LLMs for Policy, Regulatory, and Compliance in IoMT - Opportunities, Risks and Safeguards
talks.teaser: Shows how large language models can map medical device policies to HIPAA and NIST guidance, and how prompt injection puts clinical IoT systems at risk.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the state of healthcare breaches and the connected medical device attack surface in hospitals. It points to flat networks, overprivileged identities, and devices that have stayed unpatched for years, with many connected devices per bed. Availability and integrity matter because a device cannot simply be taken offline to patch it. The team's threat model showed that a poisoned retrieval knowledge base could steer a clinical AI agent into suppressing alerts or changing dosing.

The middle section reviews existing risk frameworks and finds little fit for clinical settings. The team then presents LLM-based approaches. One uses graph-based access control (NGAC) to limit what AI agents can reach, so that injected instructions cannot widen their privileges. Another is a knowledge-graph tool that compares vendor policies against HIPAA-like and NIST guidance and produces gap reports. Data security, covering encryption in transit and at rest, was described as work still in progress.

The closing part covers risks: prompt injection, hallucinated assurance, and reliance on external or cloud-hosted models. The advice is to keep humans in the loop, treat model output as untrusted input, and layer defenses rather than rely on one product. In the Q&A, the presenter explained that linking specific devices to specific control gaps can turn manual compliance review into automated risk assessment.

talks.title: Minimize Harm, Maximize Defense - How Anthropic Navigates the Offense Defense Divide
talks.teaser: Explains how Anthropic sorts cybersecurity requests into four risk categories and why its Fable 5 safety margin blocks more defensive work.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the dual-use problem that has long surrounded security tools such as mass scanners, Metasploit, Cobalt Strike and code analysis suites. The speaker, a technical policy manager for cyber safeguards at Anthropic, argues that AI sharpens this tension because capabilities arrive faster, at larger scale and to more people. Open-weight models cannot be gated, monitored or updated once released, so he frames hosted frontier models as a window in which defenders can get ahead.

The middle section walks through the written cyber constitution and its buckets: benign use that should never be blocked, low-risk dual use that is defensively biased but still blocked as a deliberate margin, high-risk dual use such as complex exploit building from binaries, and prohibited uses like self-replicating code, supply chain attacks and scaled data exfiltration. Since intent cannot be read from one exchange, Anthropic uses identity-based programs such as cyber verification and Project Glasswing as a proxy. The Fable 5 margin was set wider than for earlier models, accepting more false positives. Jailbreaks are judged with a new severity framework loosely modeled on CVSS, scoring capability gain, breadth, ease of weaponization and discoverability.

The closing part admits current shortcomings: legitimate agentic work gets blocked, independent researchers have the hardest path to access, four buckets flatten useful context, and refusal messages are vague. The speaker says the categories and thresholds will change, and invites practitioners to report blocked cases and help shape a shared industry standard.

talks.title: Pwning Agentic Browsers with PleaseFix - A New Vulnerability Class for 0 Click Takeover
talks.teaser: Shows how agentic browsers such as Atlas, Comet, Claude in Chrome and Gemini can be hijacked through poisoned pages, calendar invites and browser history.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the promise of agentic browsers: AI assistants that open tabs, click buttons and act inside sessions the user is already logged into. The speaker argues that this access is what makes them dangerous, since an attacker who controls the agent's instructions inherits the user's identity. The session introduces PleaseFix, an agent-targeting vulnerability class that evolves ClickFix, and Intent Collision, where attacker content is folded into the user's own request so the agent treats it as one plan.

The middle of the talk is a series of live demonstrations. Injected instructions spread across a page evaded per-scroll classifiers. WhatsApp Web was a hard block in one browser, but a direct request to the agent kept the sensitive-site warning soft and let messages be sent. A calendar invite with a hidden button made Comet read a password file from the local filesystem and send it out. Claude in Chrome ran attacker JavaScript from a cloned CDN and leaked email, and a 1Password flow was used to reset a password. The speaker also described HistoryFixing, which poisons browser history, a feature present in browsers for years, that agents treat as ground truth. Localhost access was used to reach a Jupyter notebook and open a reverse shell, after URL checks were bypassed with redirects.

The closing takeaway is that many vendor boundaries were soft, model-based, or bypassed repeatedly, and that the vendors responded differently, with one paying a bounty. The speaker's conclusion is that only deterministic, code-level controls stopped the attacks, so builders should not rely on model safety training alone.

talks.title: AgentBreaker A blind spot detector for your coding agents
talks.teaser: Shows how a pre-implementation security context step and a small fine-tuned model can make coding agents produce more secure code.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a shift in software development: coding agents write code far faster than humans can review it, so the bottleneck has moved to PR review. The speakers, from Corridor, argue that security should be enforced when code is generated rather than after vulnerable code is already in a pull request. They cite a benchmark result in which even a strong agent setup reached only a small share of secure solutions, though most outputs were functionally correct.

The core idea is security context retrieval. Before an agent implements a plan, a separate model identifies the security risks that the planned change could introduce, and those risks are added to the plan. On 30 SussVibes tasks, a Claude Code setup with this step raised security correctness from 36% to 52% while functional correctness stayed at 100%. To measure the retrieval step itself, the team built PreMortemBench. Frontier models scored F1 around 60 to 63%, and their latency was too high to run before every plan.

To close that gap, the team fine-tuned an open-weight Qwen model. It was faster and scored higher on their internal benchmark, with most of the gains on topics that few models retrieved correctly. The talk's broader takeaway is to measure agent harnesses on the risk axes you care about, and to weigh latency and precision alongside accuracy. The AgentBreaker framework, which extends AutoBencher to full agent harnesses, is released for that purpose.

talks.title: SADF - A Taxonomy and Evaluation Framework for Agentic Security Failures
talks.teaser: Introduces an eight-class taxonomy of agentic AI security failures and a refusal-filtered harness showing that the orchestration framework shifts compromise rates.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that many agent security benchmarks overstate success. They count an attack as successful when attack keywords appear anywhere in a model's reply, which also catches refusals that quote those keywords back. The presenter introduces SADF, a framework with an eight-class taxonomy of agentic failures covering tool calls, memory, retrieval pipelines, delegated authority and multi-agent handoffs, paired with a harness that scores only confirmed tool-execution results.

The experiments ran in a simulated environment, with several attempts per attack class. The framework wrapper changed outcomes as much as the model did. With Claude Sonnet held fixed, compromise rates ranged from about 12% under CrewAI to about 31% under SmolAgents. Memory poisoning was the hardest boundary for the Claude models, while delegated authority abuse was rare but potentially high impact. Three attack classes succeeded against every framework tested.

The practical takeaways are to evaluate the orchestration framework as well as the model, give agents bounded identities, filter outputs before they reach other tools or agents, and monitor and review tool calls. High-impact permissions, such as payments, should sit in stricter tiers. The harness and payloads are published on GitHub for teams that want to test their own agents.

talks.title: That's Not Your Agent - Why Zero Trust Can't Tell
talks.teaser: Shows why Zero Trust controls miss compromised AI agents, since prompt injection hijacks intent after authentication passes and the logs stay clean.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a gap: organisations that have adopted Zero Trust, with continuous authentication, scoped permissions and full logging, still struggle to tell a legitimate AI agent from a compromised one. The speakers argue that agents are non-deterministic and keep acting after the initial grant, so the assumptions behind behavioural baselines, IAM scoping and continuous verification stop holding. Those controls check identity and permissions, not what the agent is trying to do.

The middle section maps disclosed incidents onto a typical agentic architecture. Examples include a crafted email that led an assistant to act on hidden instructions, a Slack AI flaw where a planted prompt leaked private channel data, an agent escaping its isolation environment, and an approved tool whose definition changed into a backdoor that forwarded message history. For each, the speakers identify which control failed and why the logs looked normal.

A small simulation compares a clean invoice workflow with a poisoned one. The poisoned document rewrites the agent's instructions, and the agent then sends the data out through authorised calls while the defender dashboard stays green. The recommendations focus on runtime risk evaluation, verified agent-to-agent delegation with narrowing permissions, intent-aware telemetry sent to a SIEM, inline blocking at tool and egress points, and governance records that show which policy authorised an agent's actions.

talks.title: This Wasn't AI Generated - Principles for Breaking Generative Watermarks
talks.teaser: Shows how Google's SynthID image watermark can be stripped with light diffusion regeneration and a fast offline surrogate detector trained on paired images.
talks.summary:
The speakers examine image provenance watermarks, focusing on Google's SynthID, which Gemini checks through a verification tool. They begin with baseline tests using simple distortions such as grayscale conversion, flips and cropping. The detector resisted most of these, but screenshots passed through it reliably, and the team says the detector struggles with cropping and borders.

The main attack is regeneration: a watermarked image is noised and then lightly denoised with an off-the-shelf diffusion model. About ten steps were enough to drop Gemini's detection rate to roughly 20 percent on their set of about 100 images, while the picture stayed mostly intact. To avoid querying the live service repeatedly, the team built a surrogate detector from pairs of photos and Nano Banana edits in Apple's Pico-Banana dataset, which carry the watermark implicitly. A convolutional classifier trained on these pairs ran on a CPU in about 27 milliseconds and reached roughly 90 percent accuracy on held-out data, so attack variants could be screened offline first.

The speakers also report that removing the watermark changed how Gemini described images, sometimes producing confident claims about fictional scenes. They suggest this could matter for agent confused-deputy attacks, retrieval poisoning and facial recognition. Their takeaways favor layered provenance, common cross-vendor standards and content-level reasoning over any single watermark. They note that human quality checks were limited.

talks.title: Trust Amplification in Enterprise AI Systems - MS CoPilot Case Studies
talks.teaser: Shows how indirect prompt injection in Microsoft Copilot can turn document conversions, shared sessions and device code phishing into trusted attack paths, and introduces the Locusta toolkit.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the observation that phishing succeeds by earning trust, and that users are now trained to spot it. Enterprise AI assistants create a new channel that users are told to trust. The speaker introduces "trust amplification": attacker-controlled content gains credibility as an AI system converts, contextualizes and redistributes it.

Three Microsoft Copilot case studies follow. In the first, a Word document carrying a spreadsheet formula injection was converted to Excel by Copilot, and the payload survived into a cell that could run a PowerShell command once the user enabled content. In the second, an attacker who started a shared Copilot session could poison its responses through an injected document, so every guest who joined received a link that led to an arbitrary protocol handler. In the third, a hidden instruction made Copilot walk a user through a device code sign-in as if it were a legitimate feature. A short demo showed the resulting token granting access to files, contacts and sharing, which allowed the lure to spread to other users.

The speaker's defensive advice is to treat all AI input as untrusted, sanitize outputs before conversion, limit how long shared sessions persist, train users on AI-specific social engineering, log AI activity, and hunt for device code authentication in sign-in logs. The talk closes by presenting Locusta, an open-source toolkit for red teams and defenders to model how influence spreads through AI-assisted environments.

talks.title: What we learned from SATAN about the MYTH of Mythos
talks.teaser: Compares the 1995 release of the SATAN network scanner with today's restricted AI vulnerability tools, arguing that limiting access hurts defenders more than attackers.
talks.summary:
The talk opens in 1995, when Dan Farmer and Wietse Venema released SATAN, an automated network scanner. Critics feared that giving ordinary administrators a tool that probed networks would mostly help intruders, and the tool's name stoked the panic. The speaker argues that SATAN did not invent new capability so much as compress the time needed to find weaknesses, and that scanners later became routine.

The speaker then maps that debate onto Anthropic's Mythos model and its Project Glasswing rollout, which initially reached roughly fifty companies. Mythos reportedly surfaced a 27-year-old bug in OpenBSD. The speaker contends that gating access rarely stops capable adversaries: leaks are likely across that many organizations, and rival vendors can build comparable systems quickly, as OpenAI did within about two weeks. Earlier fights over strong cryptography and export controls on 56-bit DES show a similar pattern, and the cost of restriction falls on defenders, researchers, and organizations left off the list.

The proposed alternative is responsible disclosure, a model that has worked for about three decades by giving vendors a fixed window to fix flaws before details go public. The speaker suggests that any staged access to AI security tools should be time-limited, tied to a few patch cycles, rather than open-ended. The takeaway is that wider availability of defensive tools has tended to do more good than keeping them quiet.
